title-group.article-title: A two-step scoring model incorporating visceral-to-subcutaneous fat ratio and systemic immunoinflammatory index for predicting cytokine release syndrome severity in patients with gastric cancer receiving Claudin18.2-targeted CAR-T cell therapy

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) greatly impacts survival in patients who undergo chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy, and the identification of its determinants is still challenging. We analysed the impact of systemic immunoinflammatory index (SII) and body composition parameters derived from CT images on the severity of CRS in 45 patients with advanced gastric cancer treated with CLDN18.2-targeted CAR-T cells. The waist circumference, skeletal muscle index (SMI), skeletal muscle density (SMD), subcutaneous fat area (SFA), visceral fat area (VFA) and VFA-to-SFA ratio (VSR) on baseline CT were automatically segmented and calculated using a deep learning-based tool. The relationship between SII, body composition, and CRS severity was investigated by using ROC analysis, univariate and multivariate binary logistic regression. There were no significant differences in SMI, SMD, SFA and waist circumference between patients with CRS grade 1 and 2. CRS grade 2 patients exhibited significantly higher VSR and SII than patients with CRS grade 1 (P = 0.003 and 0.012, respectively). ROC analysis showed that the AUCs of VSR and SII for predicting CRS grade were 0.762 (0.620–0.905) and 0.721 (0.563–0.879), respectively. Logistic regression analysis demonstrated that SII > 553 × 109/L and VSR ≥ 0.21 were significantly linked with high grade CRS (P = 0.035 and 0.014, respectively). We constructed a two-step scoring CRS prediction model based on VSR and SII, and the AUC of this model achieved 0.802 (0.665–0.939) for predicting high-grade CRS in advanced gastric cancer patients receiving CLDN18.2-targeted CAR-T cell therapy, providing a practical tool for early risk stratification and clinical intervention.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: CAR-T cell therapy is gaining momentum as a treatment option [1]. Compared with conventional immunotherapy, CAR-T cells can significantly proliferate and kill tumour cells in vivo upon antigen engagement, leading to a breakthrough in therapeutic efficacy [2, 3]. However, adverse events associated with CAR-T cell therapy are also evident [4]. The activation and expansion of CAR-T cells precipitate a surge in cytokine production, thus triggering an elevated systemic inflammatory response, which may lead to a range of clinical symptoms, such as fever, hypotension and hypoxia [5]. Treatment for cytokine release syndrome (CRS) is generally controllable, and the IL-6 receptor inhibitor tocilizumab can be used preemptively to prevent toxicity after infusion [6]; moreover, oxygen and vasoactive medications may ameliorate severe CRS. Nonetheless, in certain patients, CRS may lead to severe and life-threatening disease, posing a significant obstacle in the clinical practice of CAR-T therapy [7, 8]. Therefore, there is an imperative need to explore the determinants that potentially predict severe toxicity in patients receiving CAR-T therapy.

Cachexia is commonly observed in patients with malignant diseases and is characterized by malnutrition; additionally, this disorder is typically caused by systemic inflammation and a negative energy balance [9]. Research has investigated the effects of various indicators of cachexia on the toxicity or prognosis of haematologic malignancies treated with CAR-T cell therapy. Parameters such as cachexia markers, including loss of body weight, albumin, and C-reactive protein (CRP), have been documented as prognostic indicators for patients with B-cell lymphomas treated with CAR-T cell therapy [10]. Moreover, serum albumin and total cholesterol levels are inversely correlated with the severity of CRS induced by CAR-T cell infusion [11]. Nevertheless, in patients with solid tumours undergoing CAR-T cell therapy, the relationships between body composition parameters, inflammatory indicators and CRS remain elusive [12].

Multiple studies indicate that severe depletion of muscle mass (sarcopenia) and weak muscle strength are correlated with decreased survival and high-grade immune-related adverse events (irAEs) [13–16]. Preclinical research and clinical data have shown a direct pathophysiologic link between drug therapy-induced systemic inflammatory responses and sarcopenia in various cancers [17, 18]. Furthermore, adipose tissue is a structurally and functionally heterogeneous organ. Subcutaneous and visceral tissues differ in their impacts on systemic inflammation and metabolic regulation. Large numbers of proinflammatory M1 macrophages accumulate around mesenteric adipocytes in individuals with visceral obesity, thus releasing proinflammatory factors and promoting adipocyte apoptosis. Within the realm of cell therapy, patients with elevated BMI and high visceral adiposity area may develop CRS earlier and more severely, especially those with large B-cell lymphoma treated with CD19-targeted CAR-T cells [19].

As a Claudin18.2 (CLDN18.2)-targeted CAR-T cell therapy, CT041 represents a breakthrough in patients with advanced gastric cancer (GC), with an ORR and DCR of 57.1% and 75.0%, respectively [20, 21]. Approximately 46.4% of patients in this study were reported to have grade 2 CRS, and CRS was independent of both dose and cancer type in terms of incidence and severity. This may make it more difficult for advanced GC patients to withstand severe CRS, as they have experienced multiple lines of standard therapy. Therefore, we investigated the associations of body composition parameters and conventional clinical markers with the severity of CRS and serum cytokine levels in patients with advanced GC treated with CLDN18.2-targeted CAR-T cells. Our objective was to construct a straightforward and effective CRS grading prediction model to provide an early warning for patients with high-grade CRS, enabling clinicians to implement appropriate precautions to mitigate CRS toxicity.

sec.title: Study population and design
sec.p: A total of 53 patients diagnosed with advanced GC and receiving phase I CLDN18.2-targeted CAR-T cell therapy (NCT03874897) at Peking University Cancer Hospital between March 2019 and December 2021 were enrolled. Prior to pretreatment and at least 14 days after receiving bridging therapy, these patients underwent baseline CT examinations (Fig. 1). The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) histologically confirmed advanced gastric adenocarcinoma, (2) underwent at least one line of systemic therapy, (3) immunohistochemically-confirmed moderate-to-high expression of CLDN18.2 in tumour tissues, and (4) Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance score of either 0 or 1. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) Absence of contrast enhanced venous phase CT images, (2) poor CT image quality, and (3) significant ascites interference with body composition measurements. Clinical data, including sex, age, height, CLDN18.2 expression, and metastatic sites were extracted from the medical records. The criteria for CLDN18.2 expression levels were as follows. Low expression was characterized as any staining intensity with less than 40% of cells positive or an intensity of 1 + regardless of the percentage of positive cells. A medium expression was specified for staining intensities of 2 + and 3 + with 40–69% of cells positive (inclusive of 40%). High expression was defined as intensities of 2 + and 3 + with 70% or more of the cells showing positive staining.

Data on factors reported in the literature or considered to be related to CAR-T therapy toxicity, including baseline BMI, serum LDH, albumin and creatinine concentration, were collected. All patients received diphenhydramine, acetaminophen, or an equal dose of ibuprofen 30 min before CAR-T cell infusion to prevent CRS. The ASTCT criteria were utilized to grade CRS events (Detailed CRS grading standards are shown in Table A.1) [22], and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) was not detected during this investigation. The day of CAR-T cell infusion was recorded as Day 0, and the days prior to clearance were recorded as negative.

sec.title: CT protocol
sec.p: The patients fasted for 6 h before the examination. Patients were administered an intramuscular injection of either scopolamine butylbromide or anisodamine 15–20 min before the examination to minimize gastrointestinal motility. Before the scan, the patients took 6 g gas-producing powder with 10 mL water orally to distend the stomach cavity and subsequently assumed a supine position for a full abdomen CT scan.

Enhanced CT scans were performed on GE Lightspeed 64 VCT or Discovery CT750 HD scanners (GE Medical Systems, Milwaukee, WI, USA). Non-ionic contrast agents (Omnipaque 300, 1.5 mL/kg, iodine concentration 300 mg/mL) were injected intravenously at a flow rate of 3.5 mL/s, and arterial phase, venous phase and delayed phase scans were performed 35–40, 70 and 120 s post-injection, respectively. The scanning range extended from the diaphragm dome to the pubic symphysis. Imaging parameters: tube voltage 120 kVp, detector collimation width 64 × 0.625 mm, pitch 0.984, tube current using automatic milliampere technology, range 120–550 mAs, scanning layer thickness 5 mm. Finally, the PACS workstation reconstructed the original images in the coronal and sagittal planes.

sec.title: ROI segmentation and calculation
sec.p: In this study, body composition parameters derived from CT images were used as quantitative metrics to assess the patients’ physiological conditions. We trained a 2D-UNet model based on the nnU-Net method and proposed a deep learning-based tool for automatically segmenting and calculating body composition parameters [23, 24]. The model employed axial CT images at the third lumbar (L3) vertebra level, incorporating one slice superior and one slice inferior, to calculate the average values for each parameter across three consecutive slices.

The muscle components include the psoas major, erector spinae and abdominal wall muscles. The cross-sectional muscle area was normalized by the square of the patient’s height (m2) at baseline, thus yielding a standardized muscle mass measure. Additionally, skeletal muscle density (SMD) is ascertained by averaging the CT attenuation values within the delineated muscle area at the venous phase. Adipose tissue encompasses the subcutaneous fat area (SFA) and visceral fat area (VFA), and the VFA-to-SFA ratio (VSR) offers further insight into body fat distribution. The Suzuki85 algorithm [25] was used for precise edge detection in image analysis, and the identified contours were deblurred to generate the geometric perimeter of the patient’s waist circumference (cm) at the L3 level. Figure A.1 illustrates the measurement method.

sec.title: Peripheral blood inflammation indicators and cytokines
sec.p: Prior to the infusion of CAR-T cells, lymphocytes were depleted by using the Fludarabine and Cyclophosphamide (FC) regimen. Before depletion, it was allowed for the collection of routine markers indicative of the patient’s inflammatory or trophic status, including the peripheral blood platelet (PLT), neutrophil, and lymphocyte counts. The systemic immunoinflammatory index (SII) was calculated by multiplying the peripheral blood PLT by the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio. The baseline levels of cytokines (including IL-2, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-15, TGF-β1, and IFN-γ), CRP, and ferroprotein were measured before lymphocyte depletion and were monitored according to the clinical trial protocol.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The Shapiro‒Wilk test was used to assess the normality of continuous variables. Normally distributed variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD), and non-normally distributed variables were expressed as median with interquartile range (IQR). Depending on their distribution, the Mann‒Whitney U test or independent samples t test was utilized to discern body composition parameters and clinicopathologic factors that distinguished between CRS grade 1 and 2 groups. The diagnostic performance of differential variables as well as the CRS prediction model was evaluated using ROC curve analysis, with the area under the curve (AUC) calculated alongside sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and accuracy. Optimal cut-off values were determined by maximizing the Youden index, and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated via 2000 bootstrap resamples. Potential risk variables for CRS severity were identified via univariate binary logistic regression, and independent risk factors for CRS severity were selected via multifactorial logistic regression with backward stepwise selection (likelihood ratio test). A CRS prediction scoring model was subsequently developed based on these factors. Pearson’s correlation was applied to examine associations between body composition parameters and plasma inflammatory indicators. For longitudinal data analysis, two-way ANOVA was used to examine the effects of time and group on the corresponding variables. Data analysis was conducted with IBM SPSS 26.0 and R 4.2.2. A two-tailed P value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Patient characteristics
sec.p: Between March 2019 and December 2021, 45 of 53 GC patients treated with CLDN18.2-targeted CAR-T cells at our institution met the inclusion and exclusion criteria (Fig. A.2). Table 1 presents the baseline characteristics of the enrolled patients. The median age was 49 (IQR: 40–58) years, with males comprising 53.3% (24/45) of the cohort. Given that all the patients had advanced GC, the median body mass index (BMI) was merely 18.4 kg/m2 (IQR: 16.2–21.0), and 53.3% (24/45) of the patients met the World Health Organization criteria for lean populations in Asia. Twenty-six (57.8%) of the 45 patients experienced a CRS grade of 2, whereas 19 (42.2%) underwent a CRS grade of 1. There were no patients diagnosed with CRS grade 3 or higher. CRS predominantly occurred on the first day post-transfusion (Fig. A.3), with a median duration of 6 days (IQR: 4–8). All the CRS outcomes were either resolved or recovered.

sec.title: Comparison of baseline clinicopathological characteristics and body composition parameters between patients with CRS grade 1 and 2
sec.p: Table 2 illustrates the differences between baseline clinicopathologic variables, laboratory indices and body composition parameters in different CRS grade subgroups. There were no significant differences in sex, ECOG PS, CAR-T cell infusion dose, CLDN18.2 expression, tumour burden, baseline PLT, lymphocyte, LDH, albumin, creatinine, CRP, or log10 ferroprotein between the two groups. Patients in the CRS grade 2 group exhibited significantly greater baseline IL-6 levels than those in the CRS grade 1 group (10.92 (6.28-21.10) vs. 4.84 (0.00-10.89), P = 0.038). Additionally, there were no differences in the sites of metastasis between patients in different CRS grade groups (Table A.2).

sec.p: Regarding body composition parameters, our analysis revealed no significant differences in SMI or SMD between patients with CRS grade 1 and grade 2. While SFA showed a borderline non-significant trend toward being higher in patients with CRS grade 1 than those with grade 2 (80.95 [52.09] vs. 52.71 [42.36] cm2, respectively; P = 0.051). In addition, the VSR was significantly elevated in CRS grade 2 patients than in grade 1 patients (1.07 [2.64] vs. 0.23 [0.19], respectively; P = 0.003). However, other parameters, including visceral fat area, waist circumference, and BMI, showed no significant difference between the two groups.

sec.title: Construction of a two-step CRS prediction model
sec.p: ROC curve analysis was used to assess the ability of inflammatory markers and body composition parameters to predict CRS severity. Table 3 delineates the AUC of body composition parameters classified according to the optimal threshold to predict the severity of CRS in patients. Only the AUC of VSR in predicting CRS was statistically significant, with an AUC 0.762 (95% CI [0.620–0.905], P = 0.003) (Fig. 2; Fig. A.4 illustrates two typical patients). Additionally, the AUC of SFA for predicting CRS was borderline positive, reaching 0.660 (P = 0.069). In contrast, the predictive efficacy of the skeletal muscle related parameters SMI and SMD, as well as traditional metrics BMI and waist circumference, for CRS was not significant. In terms of inflammatory markers, according to ROC curve analysis, the AUC of SII for predicting CRS grade was 0.721 (95% CI [0.563–0.879], P = 0.012, Table 3 and Fig. A.5), which was superior to baseline IL-6 (AUC = 0.680, 95% CI [0.508–0.852], P = 0.041) and neutrophil counts (AUC = 0.679, 95% CI [0.520–0.839], P = 0.042). Based on the optimal Youden index, the cutoff value for SII was set at 553 × 109/L, the cutoff value for baseline IL-6 was set at 6.44 pg/mL, and the cutoff value for neutrophil count was set at 3.66 × 109/L.

sec.p: Then we included VSR [high/low], SII [high/low], baseline IL-6 [high/low] and neutrophil count [high/low] associated with CRS grading via univariate and multivariate logistic regression. Univariate analysis demonstrated that high VSR (OR = 10.542, 95% CI [2.331–47.669], P = 0.002, Table 4), high baseline IL-6 (OR = 7.222, 95% CI [1.911–27.299], P = 0.004), high neutrophil count (OR = 4.375, 95% CI [1.139–16.904], P = 0.032) and high SII (OR = 7.200, 95% CI [1.868–27.749], P = 0.004) were all predictors of CRS grade. In the multifactorial logistic regression using backward stepwise selection (likelihood ratio test), high VSR (OR = 7.476, 95% CI [1.513–36.954], P = 0.014, Table 4) and high SII (4.914, 95% CI [1.122–21.517], P = 0.035) were ultimately identified as independent predictive factors for CRS severity. Finally, we determined to combine VSR with SII to construct a model for predicting CRS grade. We assigned a score of 1 to high VSR (0 otherwise) and a score of 1 to high SII (0 otherwise). The score calculated for each patient was subsequently utilized as a combined score to facilitate a more precise prediction of the risk of high-grade CRS in patients. The findings indicated that the AUC of the combined score for predicting CRS grade attained 0.802, 95% CI [0.665–0.939], P = 0.001 (Fig. 3 and Table A.3). Beyond its overall discriminative performance, the combined score also demonstrated meaningful risk stratification across CRS grades. Specifically, a combined score of 2 was observed in 73.1% of patients with CRS grade 2, compared with 21.1% in patients with CRS grade 1 (P = 0.001; Table A.4).

sec.title: Associations of SFA and VSR with serum inflammatory indicators
sec.p: Subsequently, we conducted a Pearson correlation analysis on body composition parameters and serum CRP, ferroprotein and cytokine levels before and after CAR-T cell infusion (Fig. 4). The findings demonstrated that the SFA exhibited a significant inverse correlation with the baseline inflammatory indicators IL-6 and IL-8 (r = −0.361, P = 0.014 and r = −0.297, P = 0.048; respectively). Furthermore, the SMD was negatively correlated with the peak IL-10 concentration (r = −0.369, P = 0.013), and BMI was inversely related to the baseline TGF-β1 concentration (r = −0.299, P = 0.046).

The median CRS duration was longer in patients with a high VSR than in those with low VSR (6.0 [5.0–9.0] vs. 4.5 [3.0–8.0] days, respectively), although there was no discernible difference between these two groups (P = 0.106). Afterwards, we compared the CRP, ferroprotein and IL-6 levels between patients with VSR ≥ 0.21 and those with VSR < 0.21 (Fig. 5). Regarding serum inflammatory markers, the baseline CRP, IL-6 and peak CRP levels were greater in patients with high VSR than in those with low VSR (P = 0.026, 0.019 and 0.002, respectively; Fig. 5). To further characterize inflammatory dynamics, longitudinal trajectories of CRP, ferroprotein, and IL-6 were analysed (Fig. 6). A significant group × time interaction was observed for CRP (Pinteraction = 0.009), indicating persistently higher CRP levels across the treatment course in the high-VSR group. Notably, a transient elevation of mean IL-6 in the low-VSR group was observed on day 3. This discrepancy was attributable to the highly right-skewed distribution of IL-6, with two patients in the low-VSR group exhibiting unusually high IL-6 peaks at this single time point (Fig. 5B). Detailed review of their longitudinal profiles revealed rapid normalization of IL-6 thereafter, and neither patient developed high-grade CRS. Consistently, additional analysis of peak IL-6 levels demonstrated no significant difference between patients with high-grade and low-grade CRS (non-parametric test, P = 0.605), suggesting that isolated peak IL-6 did not adequately reflect CRS severity.

sec.p: In contrast to VSR, SFA appeared to exert a protective effect. The baseline IL-6 level in the low SFA group was greater than that in the high SFA group (P = 0.002, Fig. A.6). This was also illustrated by the decreased levels of ferroprotein that were observed during the first week after CAR-T cell infusion in comparison to those patients with low SFA, although the interaction was not statistically significant (Pinteraction = 0.332, Fig. A.7). This discovery aligns with correlation analyses indicating a negative correlation between SFA and CRS-related inflammatory markers. Although the VFA was not directly associated with CRS severity, the ratio of the VFA to the SFA was proven to be a more effective indicator of CRS severity. This phenomenon could be ascribed to the fact that a significant proportion of the participants in this research had a low BMI.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: CAR-T cell therapy has demonstrated great potential in the treatment of GC, and the identification of its toxicity is crucial for improving prognosis [4, 26]. In haematologic neoplasms, several studies have explored the risk factors for CRS, including CAR-T cell product type, high tumour burden, high volume of infused cells, intensity of lymphodepletion, severe thrombocytopenia and high visceral fat area [27–30], yet corresponding explorations in solid tumours are less common.

Our study demonstrated that a two-step prediction model based on VSR and SII can be used to identify GC patients at risk of developing high-grade CRS after receiving CLDN18.2-targeted CAR-T cell infusion. The relationship between body composition and immunotoxicities or survival has been examined in patients with solid tumours [31]. Patients diagnosed with sarcopenia are more vulnerable to acute medical incidents, such as severe toxic events, after treatment with immunotherapy. Additionally, patients with low SMD were more prone to a poor prognosis [13]. In our investigation, the SMD in CRS grade 1 patients was greater than that in CRS grade 2 patients, but the difference was not statistically significant. A recent large-sample study also reported that the acute-phase inflammatory response was associated with sarcopenia; nonetheless, sarcopenia is merely a symptom of inflammation and not the fundamental cause [32]. This suggests that in the context of CAR-T cell therapy, sarcopenia may lack a direct causal relationship with systemic inflammation.

Adiposity appears to primarily influence the systemic immunoinflammatory response. The SFA was found to be a protective factor against CRS after CAR-T cell therapy, and the VSR was an independent predictor of CRS grade. VFA did not significantly affect the CRS grade in our study, which contradicts David et al.’s finding that the VFA is an independent predictor of CRS severity in patients with haematologic tumours receiving CAR-T cell therapy [19]. These inconsistent results may be attributed to differences in ethnicity, sample size, and cancer type. Notably, the VFA was considerably lower in patients with GC in this study than in reported cohorts of patients with B-cell lymphoma in Western populations (28.64 vs. 121.6 cm2, respectively) [33], possibly resulting in insufficient predictive effectiveness of the VFA for CRS. Furthermore, systemic inflammation is a pivotal factor in malignancy and is linked to worse clinical outcomes in patients with solid tumours. This study indicated that a high SII correlated with the severity of CRS. Consequently, we developed a two-step CRS prediction model that concurrently assessed the patient’s body composition and systemic inflammatory condition. The presence of elevated SII and VSR in the patient signified an increased likelihood of developing high-grade CRS. In critical situations like CRS, a missed diagnosis might result in rapid deterioration of the patient’s condition, thereby emphasizing the necessity for heightened sensitivity. When the model score is greater than 0 (1–2 scores), sensitivity can reach 0.962, facilitating the early identification of high-risk patients susceptible to developing high-grade CRS in clinical practice and enabling enhanced surveillance.

This study was conducted on advanced GC patients with high malignancy and depletion. Although the VFA failed to predict the severity of CRS, the AUC for the VSR in discriminating CRS grade was greater than that for the SFA, which may imply that the VFA still plays a role in lean GC patients. Adipocytes not only serve as the body’s energy reservoir but also function as active immune regulatory organs, secreting adipokines with dual metabolic and immune regulatory functions (such as leptin and IL-6) and expressing various immune-related receptors, including Toll-like receptors, IL-6 receptors, and TNF receptors [34]. The chronic low-level expression of these pro-inflammatory mediators leads to a systemic inflammatory state in the body, referred to as “meta-inflammation” [35]. Previous studies have shown that irAEs associated with acute immunoinflammatory responses are not caused by specific treatment regimens or drugs but may be related to the patient’s pre-existing inflammatory and metabolic environment [34, 36]. Additionally, adipose stem cells derived from subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) and visceral adipose tissue (VAT) have different transcriptomic profiles and exhibit varying levels of differentiation [37]. Previous studies have emphasized the opposite role of SAT and VAT in inflammation and metabolism; certain components of SAT possess anti-inflammatory properties in the context of obesity, whereas VAT tends to promote inflammation. Macrophage infiltration in VAT is significantly augmented in a mouse model exposed to a high-fat diet [38, 39]; however, this effect is rarely observed in SAT in obese individuals [40, 41]. Moreover, a significant correlation was observed between the profiles of patients with macrophage-activating syndrome and clinical symptoms of CRS [42, 43]. White adipose tissue macrophages aggregate with necrotic adipocytes, expressing activation markers and releasing cytokines that continuously trigger acute inflammatory responses [44]. Macrophage overactivation in VAT may result in abnormally high levels of IL-6, CRP and ferroprotein. CRP levels were consistently greater in patients with high VSR than in those with low VSR up to 21 days after CAR-T cell infusion in this study.

The assessment of muscle and fat based on regular CT measurements is stable and reliable, especially because it avoids the need for repeated invasive tests. Therefore, early prediction of CRS based on regular baseline CT examination combined with complete blood count may prompt clinicians to enact early preventive measures to improve the clinical outcomes of CAR-T cell-treated patients by modulating the production and release of inflammatory mediators and regulating body metabolism under stress.

There were potential limitations of this study. First, this study employed a retrospective analysis of a single-centre, prospective cohort, and it is possible that there were additional uncollected covariates that influenced the outcomes. Second, the study population was limited to patients with GC who received CLDN18.2-targeted CAR-T cell therapy, and CRS grading was concentrated at grades 1 and 2. To ensure the accuracy and applicability of the VSR, it is imperative to conduct further validation on extensive samples incorporating grade 3 or even 4 CRS. Third, the findings of this study are relevant only to individuals in the lean population with advanced GC. The cut-off values in our study were specific to certain types of cancer and geographic regions. Finally, although the two-step scoring model (score > 0) showed good sensitivity, its specificity requires enhancement. Subsequent research needs to improve the model’s discriminatory performance by incorporating more biomarkers or refining the algorithm.

In summary, this study explored potential predictive indicators for high-grade CRS in patients with solid tumours and proposed a two-step scoring model combining SII and VSR. This model has the potential to be a surrogate for CRS prediction, facilitating the early detection of immune-related inflammation in patients with GC receiving CAR-T cell therapy, thereby assisting in the optimization of treatment regimens.
